newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico tortilla price hike battle heats up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico tortilla price hike battle heats up.

text.p: Tortilla makers continued their stiff pressure to force the government to hike controled prices Wednesday, but the Trade Ministry denied it had approved an April increase in the price of the corn pancakes.
"It is not true that prices are going to be increased, it is not in the cards," Javier Herrera, a spokesman for the Trade Ministry, told Reuters.

A radio report, citing unnamed sources, said earlier Wednesday that the government had agreed to hike prices to 2.50 pesos per kilo of tortillas in Mexico City starting in April from the current 1.70 pesos. No specific date was given.
Tortillas, corn flour pancakes eaten more widely than bread, are one of the few food products with price controls still in place in Mexico.

Members of the National Corn Flour and Tortilla Producers' Chamber have been pressing for a price hike or for controls to be lifted in recent days. Tortilla makers claim they cannot cover production costs at the current controled prices.
The chamber's 37,000 members have threatened to boycott in three weeks time a government scheme that gives free tortillas to the poorest of Mexican families in a bid to twist the government's arm.

The tortilla industry and the government are in talks, but there appears to be a deadlock with the government unwilling to agree to a hike that could be seen as socially disruptive in the run up to key mid-term elections in July.

Tortilla makers from the states of Tlaxcala, Veracruz and Puebla said Wednesday they will present the government, in the next few days, a detailed study that they claim justifies the need to hike prices to 2.50 pesos per kilo.

Jesus Vargas, chairman of the Regional Chamber of Tortilla Makers of Tlaxcala, Veracruz and Puebla, told Reuters that the industry could not continue functioning with prices stuck at 1.70 pesos (22 cents) a kilo.
Vargas said his regional group had requested the government also undertake an analysis of the costs involved to realise the plight of the industry.

"It is injust that the 21 percent hike that was awarded to the tortilla in 1996 has been transfered into the profits of corn flour, Vargas said, inferring that large corn flour millers had reaped the benefits of the price hike and not the tortilla makers.
The tortilla chain starts at corn farmers and goes through corn millers, both large and small, and ends at tortilla makers, who sell the product on the streets.

Vargas insisted that the government analysis should be done on a state-by-state basis and not as a country-wide analysis because of price and cost differences in the country. Tortilla prices vary according to the region, largely dependent on the local price of corn.
The government has been moving to erase price controls on foodstuffs to move to a fully market orientated economy.
But because tortillas makes up an imporant segment of the consumer price index there has been reluctance to increase prices so as not to cause an inflation spike.
